title: Opening address and plan of the treatise
english: Most excellent Tatian, you asked me to send you a written discourse and disputation on the soul, using effective arguments or proofs, and in this matter to employ no scriptural testimonies. Scriptural teaching, though it is true and—for those who wish to think piously—more certain than any human reasoning and better suited to proving a point, is nevertheless not what you want; you want me to proceed without it. You do not ask this to satisfy yourself, since you are already so instructed that you cling to the divine Scriptures, traditions, and ordinances, and you do not allow yourself to be moved from your conviction by any human arguments. Rather, you want it to convince those who think otherwise and refuse to believe the divine Scriptures, who use their skill in disputation to circumvent and deceive people unaccustomed to such debate.

I was persuaded by these reasons not to avoid this treatise as if frightened off by some ignorance. Instead, trusting in your goodwill toward me, I have promptly complied with your command and wish. For you know, in your kindness and friendship toward me, how to bring into the light of day the things that have turned out well, and how to overlook and conceal whatever seems to have been said less correctly. Knowing this, I have boldly set myself to writing.

I will use the same method and order of inquiry that those who profess such subjects are accustomed to follow with knowledge and skill. First, then, I will propose the criterion by which the soul can be grasped according to nature. Next, I will show by what arguments its existence is demonstrated. Then, in turn, whether it is a substance or an accident. After that, in order, whether it is a body or incorporeal. Further, whether it is simple or composite. Then again, whether it is mortal or immortal. Finally, whether it is rational or lacking in reason. For these are the questions that are usually investigated in a disputation on the soul, as being most proper to it and best expressing its power and nature.

For proving and confirming the points to be discussed here, I will use, in place of proofs, those common notions by which assent is usually obtained for things that are handled by the hands. For the sake of brevity and usefulness, I will now use only those reasonings that are most effective for demonstrating the things under investigation, so that, equipped with their clear and easily grasped notions and proofs, we may be more ready to meet those who oppose us. Let the beginning of our discourse and disputation, then, be drawn from here.

orientation: Gregory opens the work by addressing Tatian, explaining why he agreed to write on the soul without scriptural testimonies and outlining the order of inquiry he will follow.

title: The criterion: knowing the soul through its effects
english: Everything we know comes to us either through the senses or through the intellect. Things that fall under the senses are sufficiently proved by the senses themselves: as soon as a sense is brought near its object, it presents us with the image and appearance of the underlying thing. But things that the intellect grasps are perceived not by themselves from themselves, but from their own actions and effects. Since the soul cannot be known from itself, it can rightly be known from its effects.

orientation: Gregory now states the epistemological criterion: things are known either by sense or by intellect; since the soul itself cannot be known directly by sense, it must be known through its effects.

title: The body moves by the soul, not by outside force or natural tendency
english: Our body moves either from outside or from inside. It is clear that it is not moved from outside, because it is moved neither by pushing nor by pulling, the way inanimate things are. Yet when it moves from inside, it does not move naturally, the way fire does. For as long as fire exists, it never ceases its motion; but a body, once it has died, stops moving, although it is still a body. Therefore, since it is moved neither from outside like inanimate things, nor naturally like fire, it is evident that it is moved by the soul, which also supplies it with life. Thus, if it is established that life is supplied to our body by the soul, the soul is also known from its effects.

title: The Soul Is a Substance
english: Furthermore, that the soul is a substance is shown as follows. First, the definition of substance fits it justly. That definition is this: Substance is that which, while remaining numerically one and the same, receives contraries in turn. That the soul, without departing from its own nature, receives contraries in turn, I believe is clear to everyone. For justice and injustice, courage and cowardice, temperance and intemperance are perceived in the soul in turn, since they are contraries. Therefore, since it is a property of substance to be the recipient of contraries in turn, and this same property belongs to the soul, the soul is therefore a substance. Moreover, since the body is a substance, the soul must also be a substance. For it is not possible that what receives life is a substance, while what supplies life is not a substance. Unless someone is so insane as to affirm that what does not exist is the cause of what does exist, or again to claim that a thing whose very existence so depends on another that it cannot exist without it is the cause of that very thing on which it depends.

title: The soul is shown to be incorporeal and therefore simple
english: I have already shown that the soul exists in our body; now we must understand how it is present there. If it merely lies next to the body, as stone lies next to stone, it follows that the soul would be a body, and the whole body would not be alive, since the soul would adhere only to some part. But if it is mixed and confused with the body, the soul is cast out from its own nature and would consist of many parts, so it would not be simple. What consists of many parts is divisible and dissoluble; what can be divided is composite; and a composite can be divided in three ways. A body added to a body increases mass, but the soul existing in a body does not make it swollen; rather, it makes it alive. Therefore the soul is not a body, but incorporeal.

Furthermore, if the soul were a body, it would be moved either from outside or from within. But it is not moved from outside: it is not moved by impulse or by traction, as inanimate things are; nor is it moved from within, as living things are. For it would be absurd to call the soul the soul of a soul. So the soul is not a body; therefore it is incorporeal.

Again, if the soul were a body, it would also have qualities perceived by the senses, and it would be nourished; but it is not nourished. Even if it were nourished, it would not be nourished bodily, as a body is, but incorporeally: for it is nourished by reason and word. Therefore it does not have sensible qualities. For justice is not discerned by the eyes, nor courage, nor other qualities of that kind, which are qualities of the soul. Consequently the soul is not a body; it is incorporeal.
Moreover, since every bodily substance is divided into animate or inanimate, let those who affirm that the soul is a body say whether they want it to be called animate or inanimate.
Finally, every body has color, quantity, and shape; but nothing of that sort is perceived in the soul. Therefore the soul is not a body.

orientation: Gregory argues that the soul cannot be a body because it does not behave like one in its relation to the body, its mode of motion, its nourishment, its qualities, or its lack of sensible dimensions; therefore it is incorporeal, and since every body is composite, the soul must be simple.

title: The soul is shown to be simple because it is incorporeal
english: From those arguments the soul is shown to be without body; from them especially it is also demonstrated to be simple. For if the soul is not a body, and every body is composite, and a composite thing consists of parts, then the soul will not be composed of many parts. Since the soul is incorporeal, it will be simple: because it is not composite, nor divisible into parts.

title: The soul is shown to be immortal because it is simple and self-moving
english: It follows that what is simple is also immortal. Here is how it works: nothing that exists corrupts itself; otherwise it would never have been constituted in the first place. Things that are corrupted are corrupted by contraries. For everything that is corrupted is dissolved; what is dissolved is composite; what is composite consists of many parts; what consists of parts consists specifically of different parts; and what is different is not the same. Therefore, since the soul is simple and does not consist of many parts — because it is neither composite nor capable of being dissolved — it follows that it is incorruptible and immortal.

Furthermore, whatever is moved by an alien motion does not have the power to live from itself, but from that by which it is moved; it endures as long as it is preserved by the force operating intrinsically from that source. But when that force ceases, the thing moved by it must also cease. Therefore, since the soul is moved by itself, it never ceases to be. These steps follow one another: what is moved by itself is always moved; what is always moved never fails; what never fails lacks an end; what lacks an end is not corrupted; what is not corrupted is immortal. So if the soul is moved by itself, as has been demonstrated above, it will be incorruptible and immortal by the force of the reasoning already proposed.

Moreover, whatever is not corrupted by its own evil cannot be corrupted at all. Evil is contrary to good, and therefore has the power to corrupt it. For the evil of a body is nothing other than passion, sickness, and death; whereas its good, on the contrary, is beauty, life, health, and firm constitution. If the soul is not corrupted by its own evil — and the evil of the soul is fear, intemperance, envy, and the like — yet none of these take away its power to live and move; therefore the soul is immortal.

title: Demonstrations that the soul partakes of reason
english: Moreover, that our soul partakes of reason can be shown by many arguments. First, it has discovered arts useful for our life. No one would say they were found rashly or by some chance, since no one can show they are idle or useless to life. If therefore the arts contribute to life's utility, and what is useful is also praiseworthy, and what is praiseworthy is acquired through reason, and the arts are the soul's own discoveries, then our soul partakes of reason.

Next, it is shown that our soul is rational because our senses are not sufficient for grasping things. We cannot reach the knowledge of things by sense perception alone. Indeed, we do not wish to remain stuck in them, and this is immediately clear from the fact that senses, unless aided by reason, cannot distinguish or discern things that are equal in shape and similar in color but different by nature. Therefore, since senses destitute of reason present false images and appearances of things to us, we must consider whether things can truly be grasped or not. And if they can be grasped, there is in us a power other than sense, and a superior one, by which we may arrive at their knowledge. But if they cannot be grasped, we shall not even attain those things that appear otherwise than they are. That things are perceived by us is evident from the fact that we apply them suitably to our uses and turn them to whatever we wish. Since it has been shown that things can be grasped by us, and this cannot be effected by senses destitute of reason, which present false opinions to us, the mind indeed will be that which distinguishes and judges all things by reason and knows things as they truly are. And the mind is the part of the soul adorned and illumined by reason. Therefore the soul partakes of reason.

Finally, because we do nothing that we have not first described and defined for ourselves — and this is nothing other than the dignity of the soul, to which the knowledge of things does not come from outside, but which itself adorns things with its own designs and conceptions, and therefore depicts and describes the thing in itself beforehand, so as to bring it forth into the open afterward. The dignity of the soul is nothing other than doing all things by reason, by which it also differs from the senses. That the soul is rational has now been demonstrated.
